title: Misinformation in Germany During the Covid-19 Pandemic: A Cross-Sectional Survey on Citizens' Perceptions and Individual Differences in the Belief in False Information
screen_reason: Three-wave cross-sectional survey of German residents (N = 3,324) that asked, on a 7-point frequency scale, how often respondents come across coronavirus information they think is false or misleading, and reports the share choosing the top category ('several times a day': 9% in June 2020, 17% in February 2021) and the share choosing 'never' (8% and 4%). Per INSTRUCTIONS section 1 a 'how often' scale counts when a share of respondents above a threshold is given, and perceived amount of misinformation in one's environment counts -> RECALL (exposure). The paper's other headline results - belief in specific false claims - are explicitly out of scope.

estimates.platform: Survey (self-reported encounters across the respondent's whole information environment; no platform restriction)
estimates.date: Three waves: 29 May-7 June 2020 (W1), 23-29 September 2020 (W2), 26 January-1 February 2021 (W3). Representative point used for this row: Wave 3, 26 January-1 February 2021.
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who report coming across coronavirus information they think is false or misleading several times a day
estimates.denominator: 1,105 residents of Germany surveyed in Wave 3 via the Respondi online panel, quota-representative of the German population for age 18-69, gender and federal state (total N = 3,324 across the three waves)
estimates.definition: Selected the top frequency category 'several times a day' on the item 'How often per week do you currently come across information on the coronavirus that you think is false or misleading?' (remaining options: every day or almost every day, several times a week, once a week, several times a month, rarely, never). Falsity is the respondent's own judgement.
estimates.misinfo_def: Respondent-defined for this item: "information on the coronavirus that you think is false or misleading". (For the separate belief items the authors state: "we used fact-checking organisations' conclusions on their veracity as our ground truth (Correctiv, 2020)".)
estimates.n: 1,105 respondents (Wave 3); 1,110 in Wave 1 and 1,109 in Wave 2
estimates.source_quote: For example, the proportion of respondents who reported seeing misinformation several times a day almost doubled, from 9% in June 2020 to 17% in February 2021. Consistent with this pattern, 8% of respondents reported never encountering misinformation in June, relative to just 4% in February 2021 (see Figure 1).
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'What were People's Perceptions of the Frequency, Sources and Topics of Misinformation...', p. 21; Figure 1
estimates.ground_truth_detail: No external verification for this item: the respondent decides what counts, the item wording being information 'that you think is false or misleading'. The study's separate belief-in-misinformation items (Waves 2 and 3) did use fact-checking organisations' conclusions (Correctiv, 2020) as ground truth, but those are belief measures and are out of scope here.
estimates.moderator_quote: "How often per week do you currently come across information on the coronavirus that you think is false or misleading?" [several times a day, every day or almost every day, several times a week, once a week, several times a month, rarely, never]
estimates.notes: TIME SERIES COLLAPSED, and the choice matters. Three independent cross-sectional waves are reported; only Wave 1 (9%) and Wave 3 (17%) are given for this statistic in the text, and the paper's headline finding is that perceived prevalence rose across waves. I used Wave 3 (February 2021) as the representative point because it is the study endpoint; an adjudicator preferring the first wave would use 9% (June 2020). THRESHOLD CHOICE also matters: 17% is the share picking the TOP category of a 7-point frequency scale, so it is a heavy-exposure share, not a 'saw any' share. The 'saw any' share would be 100 minus the 'never' share (96% in February 2021, 92% in June 2020), but R8 forbids keeping a complement I computed, so it is not entered. Falsity is respondent-defined, which makes this a perception measure rather than a verified-exposure measure.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) 'Never encountered misinformation' shares are stated verbatim (8% June 2020, 4% February 2021). These measure NON-exposure; the corresponding any-exposure shares (92%, 96%) would be complements I computed and are barred by R8, so no row. An adjudicator willing to accept a stated complement would find these the single most poolable numbers in the paper. (2) Perceived SOURCES of misinformation - 'on average 72% of respondents who reported having encountered misinformation naming this source [social media] (ranging from 68% in Wave 3 to 79% in Wave 1)', plus tabloids 41-43%, friends and family 31-36%, neighbours 29-32% - are an attribution composition among the already-exposed, not a prevalence of exposure, so no row. (3) Table 1 'perceived topics of misinformation (% selected)' (e.g. Statistics 42.6%, Origins of pandemic 42.3% in Wave 3) are topic attributions among respondents, not shares exposed to misinformation. (4) All belief figures are excluded by the instructions ('Belief in false claims does NOT' count): 'between 17% and 21% of respondents believed that a COVID-19 infection is no worse than a flu', 'between 18% and 19% believed that the government is using Covid-19 as a pretext', 'masks do not protect against infections (17% and 20% in Waves 2 and 3)', and the two ambiguous items with ~45% and ~48% 'don't know'. (5) Self-reported sharing is reported only as 'Few indicated that they would share it (4%-8% across waves and items)' - a range pooled across waves AND multiple response items, with no single identifiable numerator or denominator, and framed as what one does when UNCERTAIN whether information is true, not as observed sharing of verified misinformation. I judged it too ill-defined to enter even as range_not_point; an adjudicator may disagree. (6) Detection-competence shares (78-87% somewhat/very confident; cue use 56-65%; 46-54% check independent websites) concern skills, not exposure.

rob.design: Cross-sectional online survey, three independent waves through the Respondi panel: Wave 1 29 May-7 June 2020 (N = 1,110), Wave 2 23-29 September 2020 (N = 1,109), Wave 3 26 January-1 February 2021 (N = 1,105); total N = 3,324. Each wave quota-representative of the German population for age 18-69, gender and federal state, but explicitly NOT quota-representative for education and biased towards higher education. Respondents paid a flat EUR 1.15 for a median of about 23 minutes (IQR 16-34). No response rate is reported and no respondents were excluded from the analyses. The study was not preregistered; full instruments (German originals with English translations) are on OSF (https://osf.io/hz9yq/) and the surveys were approved by the MPI for Human Development IRB. Exposure measure: a single self-report 7-point frequency item with respondent-defined falsity, so no coding procedure or inter-rater reliability applies. The separate belief measure used 12 (Wave 2) and 14 (Wave 3) true/false statements built from publicly available false claims (Sessa, 2020) with fact-checking organisations' verdicts (Correctiv, 2020) as ground truth; two ambiguous items were dropped post hoc from the regressions. Analysis: Bayesian generalized linear models in brms/Stan with default weakly informative priors, 95% equal-tail credible intervals, respondent random intercept and statement fixed effect.
